reels.title: A function is a recipe card

beats.say: What if you could hand a friend a recipe card, instead of a cooked meal?
In Python, a function is that recipe card. Writing its name alone, with no brackets, just holds the card. Adding brackets means cook it right now.
So you can keep cards in a labelled drawer. That drawer is a dictionary. Ask for the card marked fare, and you get the steps for turning text into a number.
You can even hand a card to a sorter and say, order the pile using this rule. Functions are things you pass around, not only things you run.

check.q: In Python, what is the difference between writing to_upper and writing to_upper with brackets?
opts: Nothing, they mean the same
The name alone holds the function; brackets run it now
The name alone runs it; brackets store it
check.why: The bare name is the function object itself, like holding the recipe card. Brackets call it and give you the result, like cooking the meal.

work: Find one place in your code where an if-chain picks a behaviour, and sketch it as a dict of functions.
Say out loud the difference between f and f with brackets in a few lines you wrote.

reels.title: Passing and looking up functions

beats.say: How can Python call a function you only looked up from a dictionary?
The def statement builds a function object and binds a name to it. Then f equals to_upper copies the reference, not the code. Both names point to one object. Calling f on pune returns PUNE.
Now a dictionary. Rules maps city to str dot title, and fare to float. Looking up fare gives float. Add brackets with the text twelve point five, and you get the number 12.5.

show.title: Dict of functions
show.text:
rules = {"city": str.title, "fare": float}
rules["fare"]("12.5")  # 12.5

beats.say: A function that takes or returns a function is called higher-order. Sorted with a key, map and filter are examples. An agent loop does the same: look up the tool by name, then call it with the arguments.

check.q: After f = to_upper, what does f point to?
opts: A copy of the function's code
The same function object as to_upper
The string returned by to_upper
check.why: Assignment copies the reference. Both names refer to one function object, and nothing is called until you add brackets.

work: Write a small dict that maps column names to cleaning functions, then apply it in a loop.
Check that every sorted, map or filter call in your code passes a function without brackets.

reels.title: Three traps with function values

beats.say: Why does one pair of brackets break your sort?

show.text: One pair of brackets

beats.say: Write key equals to_upper with brackets, and Python calls the function first, with no argument, and passes its result along. You get a TypeError. Without brackets, sorted calls it once for each item.

show.title: Trap one
show.text:
sorted(xs, key=to_upper())   # TypeError
sorted(xs, key=to_upper)     # correct
show.note: pass the function, do not call it

beats.say: Second trap: lambdas made in a loop. Each one remembers the variable, not its value at that moment. After three loops, all three see the last value. Fix it with a default argument that freezes the value.

show.title: Trap two: late binding
show.text:
fs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
[f() for f in fs]   # [2, 2, 2]
fs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]  # [0, 1, 2]

beats.say: Third, dispatch tables. If a model asks for a tool name that is not in the dictionary, you get a KeyError. Use get, check the name, and never call anything the model names without an allow list.

check.q: You build three lambdas in a for loop that each return i. Why do they all return the last value?
opts: Lambdas can only return the last number
Each lambda looks up i when it runs, not when it was made
The loop deletes the earlier lambdas
check.why: Closures capture the variable, not a snapshot of its value. By the time you call them, i holds its final value. A default argument i=i freezes the value.

work: Search your code for lambdas created inside loops and add default arguments where needed.
Make every dispatch dict lookup use get with a clear error for unknown names.

reels.title: When a Python function is the wrong value

beats.say: When is passing a Python function the wrong choice?

show.text: Passing a function

beats.say: In PySpark, F dot upper is a built-in that Spark optimises inside the engine. Wrap your own Python function as a UDF, and every row travels to a Python worker and back. That is often several times slower. Prefer built-ins.
For dispatch, a dictionary beats a long if chain. Adding a tool is one line, and tests can swap in fakes. But once functions share state or need setup and cleanup, move to a class.

show.title: Dict or class?
items: Dict: one line per new tool
Dict: easy to swap in fakes for tests
Class: setup and cleanup in one place

beats.say: In agents, the dictionary is also your security boundary. Only registered functions can ever run. Keep the registry explicit, validate every argument, and log each call.

check.q: You need to upper-case a column in a large Spark job. What should you choose first?
opts: A Python UDF, because it is flexible
The built-in F.upper, so Spark can optimise it
A loop over collected rows in Python
check.why: Built-ins run inside the engine and are optimised. A Python UDF moves every row between the engine and Python workers, which costs time at scale.

work: Audit your Spark jobs for UDFs that have a built-in equivalent and replace them.
Turn any agent tool list into an explicit registry with argument validation and call logging.

reels.title: A sorting tray for your data

beats.say: Imagine a pile of a thousand trip receipts. How do you grab just the fares from completed trips, in one sweep?
A comprehension is that sweep. You tell Python three things: what to keep from each receipt, which pile to look through, and which receipts to skip.
It is like a mail sorter. Letters go in, a rule rejects some, and what comes out lands in a new tray. The tray can be a list, a lookup table, or a set of unique items.
Read it like a sentence: take the fare, from each trip, where status is completed.

show.text: Take the fare, from each trip, where completed
show.sub: It reads left to right like SQL

check.q: What does a comprehension do?
opts: Builds a new collection from a pile by keeping, transforming and skipping items
Deletes items from the original pile
Sorts the pile in place
check.why: It reads items from an iterable, optionally filters them, and produces a new collection. The original is untouched.

work: Find one loop in your code that builds a list with append and read it aloud as a sentence.
Say what it keeps, where it looks, and what it skips.

reels.title: Four shapes, one line

beats.say: One line can build a list, a dictionary, a set, or just a total. How?

show.text: One pattern, four outputs

beats.say: Square brackets build a list. Take fare from each trip where status is completed. Out of ten thousand trips, maybe seven thousand fares come back.

show.title: List
show.text: fares = [t["fare"] for t in trips if t["status"] == "completed"]

beats.say: Curly braces with a colon build a dictionary, keyed by trip id. Curly braces without a colon build a set, so the cities come out with no duplicates.

show.title: Dict and set
show.text:
by_id = {t["id"]: t for t in trips}
cities = {t["city"] for t in trips}
show.note: Colon means dict. No colon means set.

beats.say: Round brackets make a generator. Wrapped in sum, it adds fares one at a time and never builds a ten thousand item list in memory. Read it like SQL: select, from, where.

check.q: You only need the total of all fares. Which is best?
opts: sum of a list comprehension
sum of a generator expression
a set comprehension then sum
check.why: A generator feeds sum one value at a time, so no full list is built. A set would also drop duplicate fares and give a wrong total.

work: Replace one sum over a list comprehension with a generator expression.
Build a dictionary keyed by id to replace a repeated search through a list.

reels.title: Where comprehensions bite

beats.say: What goes wrong when a comprehension gets clever?

show.text: Clever is not clear

beats.say: Two for clauses are fine, like looping rows then columns. Three, and nobody can tell which loop is inner. Past that, write a plain loop.
Never use one for side effects. A list of print calls builds a throwaway list of None values, wasting memory and hiding intent. Use a for loop.

show.title: Anti-pattern
show.text: [print(x) for x in xs]
show.note: Builds a list of None just to run print

beats.say: Also, a generator can be read only once. Sum it, then try again, and you get zero. And a dictionary comprehension silently keeps the last trip when two share an id.

check.q: Two trips share the same id. What does a dict comprehension keyed by id do?
opts: Raises a KeyError
Keeps the first trip
Keeps the last trip silently
check.why: Each assignment overwrites the previous key, so the later trip wins with no warning. Check for duplicates if ids must be unique.

work: Search your code for comprehensions with side effects and turn them into loops.
Add a uniqueness check before building any dictionary keyed by id.

reels.title: When to reach for something else

beats.say: When is a comprehension the wrong tool at scale?

show.text: Fast code can still be the wrong code

beats.say: It runs in memory on one machine. A list of fifty million fares may need gigabytes of RAM. Use a generator, or stream in chunks, so memory stays flat.
The speed gain over append is modest, often a third. The real cost is Python itself. Filtering a billion rows belongs in SQL or a dataframe engine, not a Python loop.
Rule for reviews: if it needs a comment, write the loop. Readable code is cheaper than a clever line at three in the morning.

show.text: Needs a comment? Write the loop.

check.q: You must filter a billion rows from a warehouse table. What is the best choice?
opts: A list comprehension after fetching all rows
A generator over all fetched rows
A WHERE clause in the warehouse query
check.why: Filtering where the data lives avoids moving a billion rows into Python. Comprehensions are for small or already-loaded data.

work: In reviews, flag comprehensions that need a comment and ask for a loop.
Push filters into SQL before data reaches Python.

reels.title: The notepad bolted to the counter

beats.say: Why would a function remember things from the last time you used it? Odd, right?

show.text: A function that remembers?

beats.say: Think of a function as an order form at a coffee shop. Some boxes you must fill in, like your name. Other boxes come pre-filled, like medium size. You can change them, or leave them as they are.

Now the trap. Imagine the pre-filled box says, use this notepad. Not a fresh notepad each time. One notepad, bolted to the counter. Every customer writes on it, so the second customer sees the first customer's order.
The fix is simple. Pre-fill the box with nothing. Then, if it is empty, hand the customer a brand new notepad.

show.title: The fix
items: If empty, make a fresh notepad

check.q: In the coffee shop story, what causes the second customer to see the first customer's order?
opts: The customer forgot to write their name
The pre-filled box points to one notepad shared by all
The shop has too many customers
The notepad is too small
check.why: The default is created once and reused, so every call that skips the box uses the same notepad.

work: Scan your helper functions for defaults that are empty lists or dictionaries.
Explain the shared notepad idea to a teammate in one sentence.

reels.title: Defaults are built once

beats.say: You call add row with one, then with two. Why does the second call return one and two?

show.title: The surprise
show.text:
def add_row(row, batch=[]):
    batch.append(row)
    return batch

add_row(1)  # [1]
add_row(2)  # [1, 2]

beats.say: Because Python builds default values once, at the moment the function is defined, not on each call. The empty list is created a single time and stored on the function. Every call that skips that argument gets that same list.
So append in call one changes it, and call two sees the change. The list now holds one, then one and two, and keeps growing for the life of the process.
The fix is the none idiom. Default to none, which is safe because it never changes. Inside, if batch is none, make a new empty list. Now every call gets its own.

show.title: The None idiom

check.q: When is the default value in a Python function signature evaluated?
opts: On every call
Once, when the function is defined
Only on the first call
When the function returns
check.why: Python evaluates defaults at definition time and stores them, so a mutable default is one shared object.

work: Rewrite one mutable default in your code with the None idiom.
Run the broken add_row twice in a REPL and watch the list grow.

reels.title: Frozen defaults and falsy traps

beats.say: Your pipeline stamps every row with a default timestamp, yet every row shows the same time from this morning. Why?

show.title: Same stamp on every row

beats.say: Same cause. A default like now is evaluated once, at definition. It is frozen when the module loads. Use none, and call now inside the function.

show.title: Fix: call it inside

beats.say: Watch the none check. If you write if not batch, a caller who passes their own empty list gets silently replaced, and their list stays empty. Write batch is none instead.
Also, star args arrives as a tuple, and double star kwargs as a dict. Put a bare star before flags, so overwrite must be named. Then load path comma true cannot happen.

show.title: Argument kinds
items: double star kwargs is a dict

check.q: Why is "if not batch: batch = []" a worse guard than "if batch is None"?
opts: It is slower
It replaces a caller's own empty list, so their list never fills
It raises a TypeError
It only works with tuples
check.why: An empty list is falsy, so not batch swaps it for a new list and the caller's object is never updated.

work: Search for datetime.now() or uuid calls used as default values.
Turn boolean flags in public functions into keyword-only arguments.

reels.title: Hidden state is an architecture risk

beats.say: A job passes in tests, then fails in production only after a worker has run for days. Could a default argument be why?

show.text: Passes in tests, fails after days

beats.say: Yes. A shared default is hidden global state. In a long-lived worker, it leaks rows between tasks, so output depends on what ran before. It also breaks tests, which pass alone but fail in a different order.
Catch it early. Turn on the lint rule for mutable defaults, such as B zero zero six in Ruff. Prefer tuples for fixed defaults, and default factory in data classes.

Also, avoid kwargs sprawl. Ten loose options hide typos and bypass review. Use a typed config object instead. Keep keyword-only flags in public functions, since adding one never breaks existing callers.

show.title: API design
items: New keyword-only args stay backward compatible

check.q: Which choice best prevents shared-state bugs and option sprawl across a large codebase?
opts: Code review comments only
A lint rule for mutable defaults plus typed config objects
Using global variables instead
Passing everything through kwargs
check.why: Automated linting catches the trap consistently, and typed config objects make options explicit and reviewable.

work: Enable the mutable-default lint rule in CI and fix the findings.
Replace a long kwargs signature in a shared library with a typed config object.
Add a test that calls a function twice and checks the results are independent.

reels.title: A function with a pocket

beats.say: How can a function remember a value after the function that created it has finished?

show.text: Can a function remember?
show.sub: even after its creator is gone

beats.say: Picture a manager training a new barista. She tucks a sticky note into the barista's apron: always add two sugars. Then the manager leaves for good. The barista still has the note and keeps following it.

Python does this with a function defined inside another function. The inner one carries a pocket of the outer one's values, even after the outer one returns. That pocket is called a closure. Make a multiplier with two, and it will double anything you give it.
To find a name, Python searches nearest first: inside the function, then the outer function, then the file, then the built-in names. The nearest match wins.

check.q: What is a closure?
opts: A function that cannot be called twice
A function that keeps the outer function's values after the outer one has returned
A function that closes a file automatically
check.why: A closure is an inner function plus the enclosing values it uses, kept alive after the outer function finishes.

work: Find a small helper in your pipeline code that is built inside another function and name what it remembers.
Explain the four lookup places to a teammate, nearest first.

reels.title: How a closure remembers

beats.say: What does double of twenty-one actually do to know that k is two?

Calling make multiplier with two creates a local variable k equal to two. Normally k would vanish when the call ends. But the inner function mul uses k, so Python stores k in a small cell and attaches it to mul.
Now double twenty-one runs mul. Python looks for x: found locally, it's twenty-one. It looks for k: not local, so it checks the enclosing scope, finds the cell, reads two. Result: forty-two.
Each call to make multiplier builds a fresh cell. So double and triple, made separately, each hold their own k and never interfere.

check.q: After make_multiplier(2) returns, where does the value 2 live?
opts: In a global variable
In a cell attached to the inner function
It is gone and recomputed each call
check.why: Because the inner function uses k, Python keeps it in a cell tied to that function, so it outlives the outer call.

work: In a REPL, inspect double.__closure__ and read the cell contents.
Build two closures from the same factory and confirm they hold separate values.

reels.title: Nonlocal and the loop trap

beats.say: Why does a counter that simply adds one to n crash with UnboundLocalError?

Reading an outer variable is fine. But the moment you assign to a name inside a function, Python decides at compile time that the name is local. So n plus equals one tries to read a local n that has no value yet, and fails.
The fix is nonlocal n, which tells Python to rebind the enclosing variable. Each counter from make counter then keeps its own running total, starting at zero.

show.text:
def make_counter():
    n = 0
    def nxt():
        nonlocal n
        n += 1
        return n
    return nxt

beats.say: A second trap: closures capture the variable, not its value. Build three functions in a loop that each return i, and all three return two, the final value, because they share one cell. Fix it by passing i as a default argument.

show.text:
fs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
[f() for f in fs]   # [2, 2, 2]

fs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]
[f() for f in fs]   # [0, 1, 2]

check.q: Three lambdas built in a loop each return i, and all return the last value. Why?
opts: Each lambda copied i at creation
They all share one captured variable i, read when called
Lambdas cannot use loop variables
check.why: Closures capture the variable itself, not a snapshot. By call time the loop has finished, so every lambda sees the final i.

work: Search your code for lambdas or inner functions created in loops and check for late binding.
Add nonlocal only where you truly rebind, and not for reads or in-place mutation.

reels.title: Closure or class?

beats.say: When should a data engineer pick a closure, and when a class?

show.text: Closure or class?

beats.say: Closures shine for small configured behaviour: a retry policy, a rate limiter, a connection factory. One function, a few captured settings, no boilerplate.

show.title: Good closure fits
items: Rate limiter with a set pace

beats.say: But the captured state is hidden. You can't easily inspect it, and an unlocked nonlocal counter is not thread safe, since plus equals one is not atomic. If several methods need shared state, or you need to test and reset it, use a class.

chip.text: Use a lock or a class

beats.say: Distributed engines add a limit. Spark serializes your function and its captured values and ships them to every worker. Capture a large lookup table and each task carries a copy. A counter you change on a worker never updates the driver's copy. Use broadcast variables or accumulators instead.

chip.text: Broadcast big data, don't capture it

check.q: A Spark job captures a 2 GB dictionary in a mapped function. What is the best fix?
opts: Make the function a closure with nonlocal
Broadcast the dictionary so each worker gets one shared copy
Increase the number of tasks
check.why: Captured values are serialized into every task. A broadcast variable sends the data once per worker instead of once per task.

work: Review functions passed to Spark or multiprocessing for large captured objects.
Replace closure state with a class when it needs locking, testing or reset.
Use accumulators, not nonlocal counters, to count across workers.

reels.title: A label on every book

beats.say: How does a librarian shelve books by author, then by title, without comparing whole books every time? She puts a small label on each one.
In Python, that label is called a key. You hand sorted a tiny function. It looks at each item and returns the one thing to compare, like a city name or a price.
Need two rules? Make the label a pair. City first. If two cities match, fare breaks the tie. That pair is called a tuple, a small fixed list of values.

chip.text: Ties fall to the next value

beats.say: Your original pile stays untouched. Sorted hands you a fresh, ordered copy.

show.text: New copy, old pile intact

check.q: What does a key function do in sorted?
opts: Turns each item into the value used for comparing
Deletes items that do not match
Sorts the list in place and returns None
check.why: The key maps each item to the value Python compares. It does not filter, and sorted returns a new list rather than changing the old one.

work: Find one place where you sort records and name the key out loud in plain words.
Replace a hand-written comparison with a simple key function.

reels.title: One key, three rules

beats.say: How do you sort trips by city, then highest fare first, then lowest id? With one key function.

show.title: One sorted call
show.text: sorted(trips, key=lambda t: (t["city"], -t["fare"], t["id"]))

beats.say: The key returns a tuple: city, minus fare, id. Python compares tuples one slot at a time. Only when cities tie does it look at fare. Only when fares tie does it look at id.
Why minus fare? Sorting always runs low to high. Negating a number flips it. A fare of 40 becomes minus 40, which sorts before minus 10. So the highest fare comes first.
This trick works only for numbers. Strings cannot be negated, so they need a different approach.

show.text: Negation: numbers only

check.q: In key=lambda t: (t["city"], -t["fare"]), when is fare looked at?
opts: Always, before city
Only when two cities are equal
Never, because it is negative
check.why: Tuples compare slot by slot, so the second value only matters when the first values tie.

work: Write a multi-field sort as a single tuple key.
Negate numeric fields to reverse just one direction.

reels.title: The None bug and stability

beats.say: Why does xs equals xs dot sort leave you with None?

show.title: Classic bug
show.text: xs = xs.sort()   # xs is now None

beats.say: List dot sort changes the list in place and returns nothing. So you just overwrote your list with None. Use sorted when you want a new list back. Use sort when you want to save memory.
Now a trap: city A to Z, but name Z to A. You cannot negate a string. Use stability instead. Equal items keep their original order.
So sort by the secondary key first, name reversed. Then sort by the primary, city. Cities that tie stay in name order, because the second sort never shuffles equals.

check.q: To sort by city A to Z then name Z to A using two sorts, what is the order?
opts: City first, then name
Name reversed first, then city
Either order gives the same result
check.why: The last sort is the primary key. Stability keeps the earlier name order inside each city.

work: Search your code for assignments of the form x = x.sort().
Add a comment on any two-pass sort explaining why the order matters.

reels.title: When a lambda is not enough

beats.say: Is a lambda the right key for a hundred million rows? Probably not.

show.text: 100 million rows

beats.say: Python calls the key once per item, so a slow lambda costs you once per row. Itemgetter does plain field access in C, which is faster. It also takes several fields and returns a tuple.

show.title: Faster field access
show.text: sorted(trips, key=itemgetter("city", "fare"))

beats.say: Two passes using stability cost two full sorts. A tuple key with a negated number costs one. Prefer one pass when you can.
At real scale, sorting in memory breaks, because Python holds the whole list at once. Push the ordering into the database or a Spark job, where it can spill to disk and run in parallel.

check.q: Which choice best fits sorting a table too big for memory?
opts: Use sorted with itemgetter
Sort twice with stability
Push the order by to the database or Spark
check.why: Python sorted needs the whole list in memory. A database or Spark can spill to disk and parallelize.

work: Swap simple field lambdas for itemgetter on hot paths and measure.
Prefer a single tuple key over two sorts when fields are numeric.
Set a row-count threshold above which sorting moves to SQL or Spark.

reels.title: A case for your function

beats.say: How do you add a feature to a tool without opening it up and changing it?

show.text: Add a feature without opening the tool?

beats.say: Think of a phone case. The phone inside is untouched, but now it survives drops. A decorator is a case for a function. It wraps the original and adds behaviour around it.
Say you want to know how long a job takes. Instead of editing the job, you wrap it. The wrapper starts a stopwatch, runs the job, then reports the time.
You write the wrapper once. Then you put it on any function with a single line above it, the at sign and a name.

check.q: What does a decorator do to the function it is placed on?
opts: Deletes it and replaces it with new logic
Wraps it, adding behaviour around the original
Makes it run faster automatically
check.why: A decorator surrounds the original function with extra behaviour, like a case on a phone, without editing the function itself.

work: Find a place where you copy and paste the same timing or logging lines, and note it as a decorator candidate.
Explain the phone case analogy to a teammate in one sentence.

reels.title: What the at sign really does

beats.say: What does the at sign above a function actually do?

show.text: What does @ really do?

beats.say: Nothing magic. At timed above def f is just f equals timed of f. Python defines f, passes it to timed, and rebinds the name f to whatever comes back.

show.title: Shorthand
show.text:
@timed
def f(x): ...

# same as
f = timed(f)

beats.say: That returned thing is a wrapper. It accepts any arguments using star args and star star kwargs, starts a clock, calls the original, and prints the elapsed time, even if the original raises an error, thanks to a finally block.

Now a decorator with settings, like retry three. That needs three layers. Retry of three runs first and returns the real decorator. That decorator takes the function and returns the wrapper. The wrapper runs on every call.

check.q: What is the plain-Python equivalent of putting @timed above def f?
opts: timed = f(timed)
f = timed(f)
f = timed()
check.why: The decorator is called with the function, and the name f is rebound to the returned wrapper.

work: Rewrite one decorated function in your codebase without the at sign, using f = deco(f), to see the mechanics.
Write a retry decorator with three layers and trace which layer runs when.

reels.title: Why everything is called wrapper

beats.say: Why does every task in your Airflow screen say wrapper?

show.text: Why is every task named wrapper?

beats.say: Because a decorator replaces your function with the wrapper, so the name and docstring of the original are lost. Logs, tracebacks and task names all show wrapper. The fix is functools wraps on the inner function, which copies the name and docstring across.
Other gotchas. Forget to return the result, and every call quietly gives back None. Forget star args, and the wrapper breaks on any function with different parameters.

Timing with a finally block still reports when the function fails, and the error still reaches the caller. Also, decoration runs once at import time, but the wrapper runs on every call. Mixing those up causes surprising bugs.

check.q: What does functools.wraps fix?
opts: It makes the wrapper run faster
It copies the original name and docstring onto the wrapper
It lets the wrapper skip returning a value
check.why: Without it the decorated function reports itself as wrapper in logs, tracebacks and task names; wraps preserves the original metadata.

work: Check every custom decorator in your repo for functools.wraps.
Add a test that asserts the decorated function keeps its name and returns its result.

reels.title: When not to reach for a decorator

beats.say: When is a decorator the wrong tool?

show.text: When is a decorator the wrong tool?

beats.say: They are great for cross-cutting concerns: timing, retries, logging, caching. One line, applied everywhere, fixed in one place. That is why Airflow task and dag, pytest fixture and agent tool all use them.

But they hide behaviour. A retry decorator on a function that charges a card can charge twice unless the function is idempotent, meaning safe to repeat. Stacked decorators run in order, and the order changes meaning: retry outside timing measures all attempts.
Heavy logic or state in a decorator is hard to test. Prefer plain code, or an explicit helper, when the behaviour is specific to one function. Keep decorators small, and always use wraps.

show.title: Rule of thumb
items: Specific logic stays in plain code

check.q: Why is stacking order of decorators important?
opts: Python rejects the wrong order
Each layer wraps the next, so order changes what each one sees, such as what retry covers when timing
Only the top decorator ever runs
check.why: Decorators nest. A retry outside a timer times all attempts together; inside, it times each attempt separately.

work: Audit retry decorators and confirm the wrapped functions are idempotent.
Document the intended order wherever you stack more than one decorator.
Move function-specific logic out of decorators into plain, testable code.

reels.title: The calculator and the messy helper

beats.say: What if a function could quietly wreck your data, and never show an error?

show.text: Silent damage

beats.say: A pure function is like a calculator. You type in numbers, you get an answer, and nothing else in the room changes. Same input, same answer, every time.
An impure function is like a helper who answers your question, but also rearranges your desk while doing it. Run it twice and the desk ends up in a different state.
In a data pipeline, that matters. If a step crashes, you rerun it. With a calculator step, rerunning is harmless. With the messy helper, you get doubled or damaged data.

show.title: Why reruns matter
items: Impure step: rerun can double or damage data

check.q: Why is a calculator-style step safer in a pipeline that gets rerun?
opts: It runs faster
Running it again changes nothing outside it
It uses less memory
check.why: A pure step only returns an answer from its inputs. Rerunning it cannot leave behind extra changes, so retries are safe.

work: Pick one transformation step in your pipeline and ask: does it change anything besides its return value?
Write down which steps would cause damage if they ran twice.

reels.title: Two questions that make a step safe

beats.say: How can you tell if a cleaning step is safe to rerun?

show.text: Safe to rerun?

beats.say: Ask two questions. Does the answer depend only on the inputs? Does it change anything outside itself? That means globals, the caller's data, files, or network calls.
Take clean, which strips spaces and title-cases a city. The pure version builds a new dictionary and leaves the original row alone. The bad version overwrites the city in the caller's row.

show.title: clean versus clean_bad
show.note: First returns a new dict. Second mutates the caller's.

beats.say: Pure steps give three wins. Rerun them safely. Test them with a two-line assert. And run them in parallel, because Spark can ship the function to many machines. Keep reading and writing at the edges, logic in the middle.

check.q: Which function is pure?
opts: One that sets row city in place and returns row
One that returns a new dict with a cleaned city
One that cleans the city and writes the row to a file
check.why: Only the second depends solely on its input and changes nothing outside. The others mutate the argument or perform I/O.

work: Refactor one in-place cleaning function so it returns a new dict.
Add a two-line assert test for it with a sample row.
List where your pipeline does I/O and move it to the first and last steps.

reels.title: Pure on the surface, impure underneath

beats.say: Is a function pure just because it copies the dictionary?

show.text: Copy means pure?

beats.say: Not always. Copying with double-star only copies the top level. If the row holds a list, both dictionaries share that same list. Append to it, and you've changed the caller's data.
Hidden inputs also break purity. Calling the current time, a random number, or a global setting means the same row gives different answers on different runs. Pass them in as arguments instead.

show.title: Hidden inputs
items: Fix: pass them in as arguments

beats.say: Spark may retry a failed task, so your function can run twice on the same row. A hidden counter or API call inside it then happens twice.

check.q: A Spark task fails and is retried. Your function increments a global counter. What happens?
opts: The counter is incremented only once
The counter may be incremented more than once for the same row
Spark blocks the retry
check.why: Retries rerun your function on the same data. Side effects such as counters or API calls then repeat, which is why impure steps are unsafe.

work: Search your transforms for datetime now, random, and global variables, and pass them in as parameters.
Check rows with nested lists or dicts for shallow copy mutation, and use a deep copy or rebuild the nested value.

reels.title: Pure core, impure shell

beats.say: Should every function in your pipeline be pure?

show.text: All pure?

beats.say: No, but push impurity to the edges. Keep reading and writing in a thin shell, and the transformation logic in a pure core. Then retries, backfills, and tests all become cheap.
Purity has a cost. Copying a million-row batch row by row wastes memory and time. Prefer vectorised column operations, which also never mutate the source.

show.title: Cost of purity
items: Python loops are slow at scale

beats.say: Some steps must touch the world, like enrichment from an API. Don't call it per row inside a transform. Load the lookup as a table and join, and make the final write idempotent with an upsert on a key.

check.q: You need reference data from an API for each row. What is the best design?
opts: Call the API inside the transform for every row
Fetch the data once as a table, join it in a pure step, write with an upsert
Store the response in a global dict as you go
check.why: Fetching at the edge keeps the transform pure and retry-safe. An upsert on a key makes the final write idempotent.

work: Draw your pipeline and mark each step as I/O or pure, then move logic out of I/O steps.
Replace per-row API calls with a lookup table join.
Make sinks idempotent with upserts on a natural key.
